questions.q: Name three supporting characters from the Seemapuri section and three from the Firozabad section of "Lost Spring".
questions.a: Seemapuri: the barefoot boy who says "My mother did not bring them down from the shelf", the boy with mismatched shoes, the boy who says "I want shoes", the group of women in tattered saris, the gatekeeper at the club. Firozabad: Mukesh's elder brother, the bahu (daughter-in-law), Mukesh's father, Mukesh's grandmother, Savita, the old woman beside Savita, the old man with flowing beard, the group of young men discussing cooperatives. A wrong answer (e.g., naming only protagonists or characters from other chapters) reveals the student cannot distinguish supporting cast from main characters or cannot locate characters in the correct narrative setting.

questions.q: Explain how the boy who says "I want shoes" in Seemapuri functions as a thematic foil to Saheb.
questions.a: The boy who says "I want shoes" explicitly voices the desire Saheb feels but cannot articulate; his direct statement "I want shoes" contrasts with Saheb's resigned acceptance of barefoot tradition ("It is not lack of money but a tradition to stay barefoot"). This foil highlights the theme of suppressed dreams: the boy's articulated wish makes Saheb's silence more tragic. A wrong answer that merely describes the boy's poverty without comparing him to Saheb shows the student treats characters in isolation rather than as thematic mirrors.

questions.q: The grandmother in Firozabad says, "Can a god-given lineage ever be broken?" Identify the literary device and explain how this line characterizes the caste system's psychological grip.
questions.a: The line uses a rhetorical question to characterize caste as an unbreakable divine ordinance. By framing caste as "karam" (destiny) and "god-given lineage," the grandmother internalizes oppression, making resistance seem sacrilegious. This reveals how caste operates not just through external force but through internalized belief. A wrong answer that only identifies "rhetorical question" without explaining its thematic effect shows surface-level device-spotting without analytical depth.

questions.q: Compare the bahu (Mukesh's brother's wife) and the old woman beside Savita. How do both characters illustrate the gendered dimension of poverty in Firozabad?
questions.a: Both women are trapped by patriarchal customs: the bahu veils before male elders and manages the household at a young age, while the old woman has "bangles on her wrist, but no light in her eyes" and says she has not enjoyed a single full meal. The bangles — symbol of suhaag — become ironic shackles; their labour produces the very symbol of married auspiciousness that marks their subjugation. A wrong answer that describes their chores without linking to the symbolism of bangles or the intersection of gender and caste misses the socio-cultural critique.

questions.q: The young men in Firozabad say, "Even if we get organised, we are the ones who will be hauled up by the police... for doing something illegal." Evaluate whether this statement reflects fatalism or realistic assessment of power structures.
questions.a: It is a realistic assessment grounded in lived experience: the nexus of sahukars, middlemen, police, and politicians ("vicious circle") has historically crushed collective action. Their fathers' fatigue and the absence of a leader confirm structural barriers, not mere apathy. Calling it "fatalism" blames the victims; the text shows systemic violence ("beaten and dragged to jail"). A wrong answer that labels them "lazy" or "unwilling to change" ignores the textual evidence of state-corporate collusion and reveals a middle-class bias.

questions.q: Write a 50-word diary entry from the perspective of the gatekeeper who lets Saheb use the swing, revealing his own conflicted position.
questions.a: "Let the ragpicker boy on the swing today. He grins like he owns the club. I open the gate, but the fence stays. My job is to keep his kind out; my heart lets him in. The tennis shoes on his feet — discarded, holey — fit him better than the players. Who am I guarding?" A poor answer writes a generic sympathy note without the gatekeeper's specific complicity (opening gate but maintaining fence) or the irony of the shoes, showing inability to inhabit a minor character's limited agency.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Supporting characters in "Lost Spring" are the secondary figures who surround the protagonists (Saheb and Mukesh) and function as narrative mirrors, thematic foils, or ______ of systemic forces (poverty, caste, exploitation, apathy) that entrap the children.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are a journalist interviewing people in ______ and Firozabad.
What is Supporting characters in "Lost Spring"? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Supporting characters in "Lost Spring" are the secondary figures who surround the protagonists (Saheb and Mukesh) and function as narrative mirrors, thematic foils, or representatives of systemic forces (poverty, caste, exploitation, apathy) that entrap the children.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can identify at least four distinct supporting characters/groups, explain their specific narrative function (foil, mirror, symbol, agent of oppression), and write a structured PEEL-paragraph linking a supporting character to a major theme (child labour, caste, lost dreams) with textual evidence.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine you are a journalist ______ people in Seemapuri and Firozabad.
